settings.text: Is this permanent now? Is this just my face?

settings.content: For most women — and this is the true answer, so hold onto it — no. It isn’t permanent. It improves substantially on its own, usually across six to twelve months, and often turns when your period returns — the hormonal side signaling it’s done. A minority find it doesn’t fully go, and manage it rather than beat it.
The best answer to this I found in three thousand posts wasn't written by a doctor. It was one line, from a woman on her third baby, and four hundred people had read it before I did:

settings.quote: "I did 18 months with my third and it took my face a full year to recover."

settings.content: A full year. Said plainly, without drama, by someone already out the other side. I read that and cried, honestly — half from relief, half because of the part they always leave out. The part that made me stop reading and start building.

Your hormones finish on their own schedule. Your barrier doesn't.

Skin that spends a year being set off by ordinary things gets better at being set off by ordinary things — the reactions grow easier to trigger, not harder. And you're running that year on broken sleep, which directly raises the enzyme sitting at the center of all of this. That has been measured. It isn't a wellness metaphor.

settings.text: So the real question was never treat it versus wait it out. It's what your face spends the waiting doing.

settings.content: Which is the exact moment I stopped reading, and started asking a different question altogether: was there any way to put back what left?
